stem:
A 4-year-old with three days of watery stools weighs 18 kg. Skin turgor is doughy. You diagnose moderate (5%) hypernatraemic dehydration and will replace the deficit over 48 hours plus maintenance.

| Test | Result | Reference |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sodium | 165 mmol/L | 135–145 mmol/L |

Which hourly rate should she receive?

options.label: A
options.explanation: Maintenance by 4-2-1 is 40 + 16 = 56 mL/hr. A 5% deficit of 18 kg is 900 mL; spread over 48 hours that is 18.75 mL/hr. 56 + 18.75 ≈ 75 mL/hr. Faster rates risk a rapid sodium fall and cerebral oedema.

options.label: B
options.explanation: That rate over-replaces (roughly 10% deficit in 24 hours plus maintenance) and would drop the sodium too fast.

options.label: C
options.explanation: 154 mL/hr is in the bolus-plus-rapid-replacement range and is unsafe in hypernatraemic dehydration.

options.label: D
options.explanation: 94 mL/hr replaces the deficit over 24 hours (56 + 900/24 = 93.5). In hypernatraemia the deficit is stretched over 48 hours, not 24.

options.label: E
options.explanation: 56 mL/hr is maintenance alone and ignores the 900 mL deficit. She remains dehydrated.

context:
Hypernatraemic dehydration: doughy skin, high Na. Replace deficit slowly (typically 48 hours) plus maintenance so sodium falls no faster than about 0.5 mmol/L/hour.

18 kg, 5% deficit: 56 mL/hr maintenance + 18.75 mL/hr deficit ≈ 75 mL/hr.
